docs.title: Welcome to VRUnited
docs.text:
VRUnited is a virtual reality (VR) application developed by the Event Lab (University of Barcelona) that supports multiple people simultaneously interacting in the same shared environment. It serves as a platform for delivering shared virtual experiences, functioning as a customized Metaverse.

The platform has been successfully used for a variety of remote applications, including virtual meetings, conferences, concerts, interactive games (like remote chess), and even professional journalistic interviews. A notable use case involved a two-hour interview for the Financial Times, conducted in a virtual restaurant with the interviewer in London and the interviewee in New York (read more about this in our academic publication).

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
VRUnited is designed to meet several crucial requirements for successful collaborative virtual environments:

  • Simultaneous Presence: Multiple participants can be present in the same virtual space, perceiving the same events from their own unique embodied perspectives.
  • Realistic Embodiment: Participants are represented by 3D virtual human avatars that closely resemble their real-world appearance. Using state-of-the-art deep learning methods, the system can automatically generate a realistic avatar from just a single frontal RGB image in about 30 minutes.
  • Cross-Platform Body Tracking: The platform utilizes the QuickVR library, adapting automatically to the tracking data provided by different VR devices. It tracks head and hand movements using inverse kinematics and can also track feet, fingers, eyes, or facial expressions if the hardware supports it.
  • Object Interaction: Participants can intuitively interact with virtual objects (such as grabbing and "eating" virtual sushi). The state of these objects is seamlessly synchronized across all clients in the environment.
  • Robust Networking: VRUnited uses the Photon Network engine to manage client synchronization, ensuring low latency and a persistent, consistent world state across all connected users.

docs.title: Cross-Device Compatibility
docs.text:
While VRUnited has been extensively tested on the most common head-mounted displays on the market—such as Meta Quest, Pico, and Oculus Rift—its underlying architecture is highly adaptable. Because QuickVR (and therefore VRUnited) is built on top of the Unity XR Plugin framework, it should natively run on any device supported by the Unity XR Plugin, including all OpenXR compatible devices (such as HTC VIVE or Valve Index).

Additionally, while a VR headset is highly recommended for a fully immersive experience, it is not strictly required. VRUnited can also be used on a standard PC in Desktop mode. This allows users without VR hardware to join and interact in the same shared environment, ensuring accessibility for everyone (though with a reduced level of immersion).

Using the VRUnited SDK, developers can easily expand upon the official distribution to add custom scenarios, avatars, and interactions.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
If you want to learn more about the technical details, the development of the platform, and the specific use case, you can read our published papers:

  • Oliva, R., Beacco, A., Gallego, J., Gallego Abellan, R., & Slater, M. (2023). The Making of a Newspaper Interview in Virtual Reality: Realistic Avatars, Philosophy, and Sushi. IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications, 43(6), 117-125.
  • Oliva, R., Beacco, A., Navarro, X., & Slater, M. (2022). QuickVR: A standard library for virtual embodiment in unity. Frontiers in Virtual Reality, 3:937191.

Next Steps: Ready to create your own Metaverse? Check out our Setup Guide to download the template and configure your project.

docs.title: Asset Management Overview
docs.text:
In VRUnited, adding new content—primarily Avatars and Scenarios (environments)—is a core part of customizing your Metaverse experience. The platform is designed to be highly flexible, allowing developers to manage and distribute these assets in two distinct ways: Local Assets and Remote Addressables.

Understanding the difference between these two methods is crucial for optimizing your application's file size, loading times, and update frequency.

docs.title: 1. Local Assets (Embedded)
docs.text:
Local assets are integrated directly into your Unity project and compiled along with the application. When you build the .apk (or executable), these assets are packed inside it.

The VRUnited template comes with a set of default local assets (such as the base avatars and the sample scene) to get you started immediately.

  • Pros:
    • Simpler to set up.
    • No internet connection is required to load the assets once the app is installed.
    • Content is guaranteed to be available instantly.
  • Cons:
    • Every new avatar or scenario increases the final file size of the application.
    • Updating, adding, or removing assets requires building a completely new version of the app and forcing users to download the full update.
  • Best used for: Core assets that will never change (like basic menus, default avatars, or the main lobby), offline applications, or projects with a small, fixed amount of content.

Learn how to add Local Assets ->

docs.title: 2. Remote Addressables (Cloud/Server Distribution)
docs.text:
VRUnited supports Unity's Addressables system, which allows you to store your heavy assets (like complex avatars or detailed environments) on a remote server or cloud storage. The application only downloads these assets on demand when the user needs them.

  • Pros:
    • Keeps the initial application download size very small.
    • Dynamic Updates: You can add new avatars or scenarios, or modify existing ones, on the server. Users will see the new content the next time they open the app without needing to download a new version of the app itself.
  • Cons:
    • Requires setting up a hosting server (e.g., AWS S3, Google Cloud, or a local server for testing).
    • Users must have an active internet connection to download new content.
    • Slightly more complex initial setup in Unity.
  • Best used for: Expanding Metaverses, applications that receive frequent content updates, or projects with a massive library of avatars and scenarios that would make a local build too large.

Learn how to configure Remote Addressables ->

Choose the methodology that best fits your project's scope, or use a hybrid approach: keep your core experience local and distribute seasonal or heavy content via Addressables!

docs.title: Adding Local Assets
docs.text: In this section, we will cover how to add custom avatars and scenarios locally to your VRUnited project. These assets will be included directly in your application build.

docs.title: 1. Adding Local Avatars
docs.text:
• In the top menu, go to Assets > Import Package > Custom Package... and select your custom avatar package to import it into your project.
  • A quick way to locate the VRULocalAvatars asset is to open the PhotonGameLogic scene (the initial scene containing the main VRUnited logic). In the Hierarchy, select the GameManager object located under __SingletonManagers__.
  • In the Inspector for the GameManager, you will see attributes referencing both the local avatars and local scenes assets. Clicking on the local avatars attribute will automatically highlight and locate the VRULocalAvatars asset in your Project window.
  • Select the VRULocalAvatars asset. In the Inspector, expand the Avatars list and increase its size to add a new element. Drag and drop your custom avatar prefab from the Project window into the new empty slot.
  • Configure Avatar Settings: For the newly added avatar, you must configure two key properties:
    • Address: A unique alphanumeric identifier for this avatar. Ensure it does not match any existing avatar addresses. This code is used to unlock the avatar during the avatar selection phase.
    • Is Locked: A checkbox that indicates whether the avatar is locked by default. If it is locked, users must input the Address code in the avatar selection screen to unlock it. If it is unlocked (unchecked), the avatar is available to be selected right from the start without requiring any code.

docs.title: 2. Adding Local Scenes (Environments)
docs.text:
• Import your custom scene package using Assets > Import Package > Custom Package....
  • Similar to the avatars, you can quickly find the VRULocalScenes asset by selecting the GameManager in the PhotonGameLogic scene and clicking on the local scenes attribute in the Inspector.
  • Select the VRULocalScenes asset. In the Inspector, expand the Scenes list and increase its size to create a new entry.
  • Configure the Scene Settings properties for the new entry:
    • Name: This must exactly match the filename of your local scene.
    • Display Name: The descriptive name that will be shown during the environment selection phase. It does not need to match the filename.
    • Thumbnail: A representative image of the scene used for quick identification in the selection menu. This can be left empty and added later.
  • Navigate to File > Build Profiles. Ensure your new scene is added to the Scene List by dragging it into the window or clicking Add Open Scenes while the scene is active.

docs.title: 3. Configuring Spawn Points
docs.text:
• Open your newly imported custom scene in the Unity Editor.
  • In the Hierarchy, create an Empty GameObject (e.g., MySpawnPoints) to organize your spawn locations.
  • Create another Empty GameObject as a child of the previous one (e.g., Spawn_00).
  • Select Spawn_00, click Add Component in the Inspector, and search for the VRU Spawnner Point script to attach it.
  • Use the Move Tool to position the Spawn_00 object exactly where you want the player to appear within the room.
  • Configure the VRU Spawnner Point attributes in the Inspector:
    • Initial Pose: Defines the starting pose of the avatar (e.g., whether they will appear sitting or standing).
    • Reserved For: A list containing the IDs (Addresses) of the avatars for which this spawn point is reserved. If the list is empty, any avatar can use this spawn point. If it contains one or more elements, only avatars with those matching Addresses can spawn here.
  • Repeat this process (creating additional child objects like Spawn_01, Spawn_02, etc.) to define all the spawn points needed for the maximum number of players the scene supports. For example, if your scene is designed for up to 4 players, you must define 4 separate spawn points.

docs.title: 4. Testing Local Assets
docs.text:
• Press the Play button in the Unity Editor to test the project.
  • Select either Multiplayer or Solo mode from the starting menu. Choose Multiplayer if you want to test the scene and multiple spawn points with other users, or Solo if you want to explore the environment by yourself without other players.
  • In the Avatar Selection screen, you will stand in front of a mirror reflecting your currently selected avatar. If you are using a VR headset, you are embodied in this avatar and can move your virtual body using your physical movements and VR controllers.
  • Use the arrows next to the mirror to cycle through your unlocked avatars. If the avatar you want to test is locked, click the Add Avatar button and input its unique ID (Address). It will immediately become available for selection.
  • Once you are happy with your choice, click the Select button to confirm your avatar and proceed to the next phase.
  • Click on Create Room to begin setting up your virtual space.
  • On the Environment Selection screen, look for your new custom scene, ensure it appears with its assigned thumbnail, and select it.
  • Finally, enter a name for your room (e.g., "Test") and complete the creation process.
  • You will load into the room. Confirm that your avatar spawns correctly at the designated spawn point and with the correct initial pose.

docs.title: Adding Remote Assets (Addressables)
docs.text: In VRUnited, Remote Assets are distributed using Unity's Cloud Content Delivery (CCD) system. Unlike Local Assets, which are embedded directly into the application build, Remote Assets are stored on a cloud server and downloaded on-demand when a user requests them. This approach keeps the initial download size of your application small and allows for dynamic content updates without requiring users to install a new version of the app.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The VRUnited remote asset architecture is designed to be highly scalable and relies on two distinct roles:

  1. The Consumer (Main Project): The core VRUnited application. It acts purely as a consumer. It does not contain the original prefabs or heavy files of the remote assets. Instead, it queries the cloud to discover available content and downloads it dynamically.
  2. The Producers (Secondary Projects): Separate Unity projects where developers create, configure, and build new custom avatars or environments. Once built, these projects upload their resulting Addressable packages (AssetBundles and catalogs) directly to Unity Cloud.

docs.title: Unity Cloud Content Delivery (CCD) Structure
docs.text:
To link the producers and the consumer, we use Unity CCD. The structure mimics a traditional web server:

  • Project & Environment: A single Unity Cloud Project and Environment (e.g., production) acts as the root directory.
  • Buckets (Sub-projects): Inside the environment, every producer project creates its own independent "Bucket" (e.g., avatars, restaurant_scene). This ensures updates from one project do not overwrite assets from another.
  • Platform Paths: Within each bucket, assets are separated by platform using dynamic paths (e.g., StandaloneWindows64/ or Android/).

docs.title: Configuring the Main Project (Consumer)
docs.text: The main VRUnited project acts as the consumer of the remote assets. It does not need the original prefabs or the CCD upload tools. Instead, it dynamically discovers and downloads content from Unity Cloud Content Delivery using a Service Account.

docs.title: 1. Create a Service Account
docs.text:
To allow the main project to securely query the Unity Cloud API and discover your remote buckets, you must create a dedicated Service Account.

  • Log into the Unity Cloud Dashboard and select the Unity Cloud Project you created during the "Setting Up CCD" phase.
  • Access your organization's administration profile. To do this, click the button with your organization's name in the top right corner to open the dropdown menu, and select Manage organization.
  • In the left-hand navigation menu, select Service accounts.
  • Click the + New button in the top right corner.
  • Give the service account a descriptive name (e.g., ccd-manager) and click Create.

docs.title: 2. Generate and Store Keys
docs.text:
Once the Service Account is created, you must generate the security keys required for authentication.

  • In the Service Account details page, locate the Keys section and click + Add key.
  • A dialog will appear displaying the new Key ID and the Secret key.
  • Crucial Step: You must copy and save the Secret key immediately (e.g., in a temporary Notepad file). For security reasons, Unity will never display this Secret key again once you close the dialog.
  • Click Done.

docs.title: 3. Assign Permissions
docs.text:
For the Service Account to function, you must grant it specific roles to access your project's Cloud Content Delivery data.

  • Scroll down on the Service Account page to the Organization roles section.
  • Click + Manage organization roles.
  • Under the LiveOps category, check the Cloud Content Delivery API Public Editor role and click Save.

docs.title: 4. Check Remote Assets Access
docs.text:
With the credentials ready, you must configure the VRUnited main project to use them for discovering the remote environments.

  • Open the main VRUnited Unity project.
  • Navigate to VRUnited > Test CCD Connection from the top menu.
  • A custom window will appear. Input your Project ID and Environment ID (these can be found in the Cloud Dashboard under your project's CCD settings).
  • In the Service Account section, input the Key ID and the Secret Key you generated in Step 2.
  • Click the Test Connection & List Buckets button.
  • If successful, the window will list the buckets found in your cloud environment. Click List Latest Release Files to verify that your uploaded .hash and .bundle files are properly discovered.

docs.title: 5. Configure the Server Path
docs.text:
Finally, you must permanently store these connection settings in the project so the dynamic loading system can find the remote catalogs at runtime. VRUnited handles this through a dedicated configuration asset.

  • In the Project window, navigate to your Resources folder and locate the QuickAddressablesSettings object.
  • This asset contains a list of ServerPathData configurations. Each path definition includes:
    • Environment: Specifies where this path is valid (e.g., Editor, Build, or Both).
    • Server Type: A dropdown to select the distribution method:
      • Local: Uses a local path on the device (can be relative to the Assets/ folder). Ideal for testing.
      • PHP Server: (Legacy) The old remote distribution system. (Not recommended for new assets).
      • Unity Cloud: The new dynamic remote asset system using CCD.
  • In the Inspector, create a new server path and set its Server Type to Unity Cloud.
  • When Unity Cloud is selected, the generic Path field is replaced by specific cloud credential fields. Input your Project ID, Environment ID, Service Account Key ID, and Service Account Secret Key. The QuickAddressablesManager will automatically use these attributes to build the correct remote URL dynamically at runtime to locate and load the catalogs.

docs.title: 6. Checking Remote Assets in Play Mode
docs.text:
To verify the entire workflow, run the application in the Editor. We will test loading both a remote avatar and a remote scene simultaneously.

  • Press the Play button in the Unity Editor.
  • Navigate through the VRUnited main menu and select ether Solo mode or Multiplayer, in case that you want to test it with multiple participants.
  • When you reach the Avatar Selection screen, you can unlock avatars by their ID. In order to do so, select Add Avatar and in the text field, input the exact ID of the remote avatar you configured earlier (e.g., albert). When you are happy with your avatar, click on Select.
  • Proceed to create a virtual room by selecting Create Room. Then select the environment that will be used for this session. Your remote scene (e.g., My Pantheon) should now appear automatically discovered alongside the local basic scenes that you have defined.
  • Click on the remote scene (My Pantheon).
  • The application will dynamically connect to the CCD, download the necessary .bundle files for both the scene and the avatar, and instantiate them together. You should now see your remote character correctly loaded inside your remote environment.

docs.title: Configuring Secondary Projects (Producers)
docs.text: Secondary projects (also known as Producers) are standalone Unity projects where developers create, configure, and compile custom avatars or environments. Once compiled, these assets are uploaded to Unity Cloud Content Delivery (CCD) so the main VRUnited application can download them dynamically.

docs.title: 1. Creating the CCD Bucket
docs.text:
To prevent assets from different secondary projects from overwriting each other, you must create an independent Bucket for each producer project.

  • Log into the Unity Cloud Dashboard and select your main VRUnited project.
  • Navigate to LiveOps > Cloud Content Delivery.
  • In the top-right corner, click Create Bucket.
  • Name the bucket after the specific content you are producing (e.g., MyRemoteEnvironments) and complete the creation process.

docs.title: 2. Bucket Initialization
docs.text:
Before configuring Unity, you must initialize the newly created bucket. This step is mandatory. Since the bucket was just created, it does not have any active Releases. Without at least one Release, the Cloud Dashboard will not generate the internal metadata (Project ID, Environment ID, Bucket ID) that you will need later to configure your Addressables.

To force the creation of the first Release and reveal these IDs, you must upload a dummy file:

  • In the Dashboard, open the bucket that you created in the previous step.
  • Click the Upload content using the dashboard option (or click "Upload Files").
  • Drag and drop any small, temporary file from your computer (e.g., a simple text file named MyDummyFile.txt) into the drop area.
  • Once the upload finishes, a "Create Release" dialog will appear. Click Submit to confirm.
  • Wait a few seconds for the Dashboard to refresh. You should now see the Release 1 badge and, more importantly, a new section detailing your Project ID, Environment ID, and Bucket ID.

Now that you have access to the necessary IDs, you must clean up the bucket to ensure it remains strictly for your project assets:

  • In the dashboard, click Remove All Entries.
  • Click Create Release again and confirm to generate a new empty Release (e.g., Release 2). Your bucket is now empty and properly initialized with all its IDs exposed.

docs.title: 3. Installing the VRUnited SDK
docs.text:
With the cloud bucket initialized, the next step is to configure your local Unity editor to handle remote asset creation. To do this, you must install the VRUnited SDK, which contains the automatic CCD configuration tools.

  • Open your secondary Unity project, i.e., the Addressables producer.
  • Navigate to Window > Package Manager.
  • Click the + icon in the top-left corner and select Add package from git URL...
  • Input the VRUnited SDK repository URL:
https://github.com/vrunited/vrunited.sdk.git
  • Click Install to proceed with the package installation. Wait for the process to finish.

docs.title: 4. Configuring the Addressables Profile
docs.text:
To ensure files are organized by platform (Windows vs Android) without overwriting each other, use the custom CCD configuration tool included in the VRUnited SDK.

  • From the top menu, go to VRUnited > Init Addressable Settings. This action automatically creates the VRUnited profile and initializes the required labels (VRUSceneSettings and VRUAvatar).
  • Go to Window > Asset Management > Addressables > Profiles and ensure the newly created VRUnited profile is set as the active profile.
  • In the profile settings, select Custom from the dropdown menu for both Local and Remote paths.

  • From the top menu, go to VRUnited > CCD Configuration.
  • A custom window will appear. Input the Project ID, Environment ID, and Bucket ID matching the bucket you initialized in Step 2.

  • Leave the Release ID field empty to automatically target the latest version.
  • Click Apply to Addressables Profile. This will modify the Remote.LoadPath to automatically point to your bucket, and [BuildTarget] macro is used ensuring builds are strictly separated into StandaloneWindows64/ and Android/ paths during compilation.
  • Once the CCD Settings are applied, go to Window > Asset Management > Addressables > Settings.
  • In the Inspector, locate the Catalog section.
  • Ensure the Build Remote Catalog checkbox is enabled.
  • Verify that both Build & Load Paths dropdowns just below it are set to Remote.

docs.title: 5. Create Addressables Group
docs.text:
Before marking specific assets as Addressables, you must create a dedicated Group configured to handle remote compilation and distribution.

  • Navigate to Window > Asset Management > Addressables > Groups.
  • Ensure that you have the VRUnited Profile selected.
  • In the Addressables Groups window, click on Create > Group > Packed Assets to generate a new empty group.
  • Rename the newly created group to something descriptive (e.g., MyRemoteAssets).
  • Select your new group (MyRemoteAssets).
  • In the Inspector window, under the Content Packing & Loading section, ensure Build & Load Paths is set to Remote.
  • Leave the Advanced Options section with the default values.

docs.title: 6. Configure Remote Scene
docs.text:
Once your Addressables group is ready, you must prepare the actual Unity Scene that will be distributed remotely. This process is exactly the same as configuring a local scene, requiring the setup of valid spawn points for the avatars.

  • Open the scene that you want to distribute (e.g., RomanPantheon).
  • In the Hierarchy, create an Empty GameObject (e.g., __SpawnPoints__) to organize your spawn locations.
  • Create another Empty GameObject as a child of the previous one (e.g., SpawnPoint_00).
  • Select SpawnPoint_00, click Add Component in the Inspector, and search for the VRU Spawner Point script to attach it.

  • Use the Move Tool to position the Spawn_00 object exactly where you want the player to appear within the room.
  • Configure the VRU Spawnner Point attributes in the Inspector:
    • Initial Pose: Defines the starting pose of the avatar (e.g., whether they will appear sitting or standing).
    • Reserved For: A list containing the IDs (Addresses) of the avatars for which this spawn point is reserved. If the list is empty, any avatar can use this spawn point. If it contains one or more elements, only avatars with those matching Addresses can spawn here.

  • Repeat this process (creating additional child objects like Spawn_01, Spawn_02, etc.) to define all the spawn points needed for the maximum number of players the scene supports.

docs.title: 7. Create Scene Addressables
docs.text:
With your remote scene properly configured with spawn points, you must now create a settings descriptor for it, mark both as Addressables, and assign them to your remote group.

  • First, locate your configured scene (e.g., RomanPantheon) in the Project window.
  • Right-click anywhere in the project folder and navigate to Create > VRUnited > Scene Settings to generate a new settings object.
  • Rename this new object descriptively (e.g., RomanPantheonSceneSettings).
  • Select the newly created VRUSceneSettings object and configure its properties in the Inspector:
    • Scene: Drag and drop your actual remote scene (RomanPantheon.unity) into this field.
    • Address: This is the internal ID. It must strictly match the exact filename of your scene (in this case, type RomanPantheon).
    • Display Name: The friendly name that will appear in VRUnited's UI environment selector (e.g., My Pantheon). This does not need to match the filename.
    • Thumbnail: (Optional but recommended) A representative image of the scene that will be displayed in the VRUnited menu.

  • Now, select both the scene file (RomanPantheon) and the settings object (RomanPantheonSceneSettings) in the Project window and drop both assets into your newly created remote group (e.g., MyRemoteAssets).
  • Crucial Step: In the Addressables Group window, ensure the Address string for the settings object is simplified to match its own filename exactly (RomanPantheonSceneSettings), and the Address for the scene matches its filename (RomanPantheon).
  • Finally, with the settings object selected in the Addressables window, click the dropdown in the Labels column and apply the VRUSceneSettings label. This allows the main project to discover it as a valid environment.

docs.title: 8. Create Avatar Addressables
docs.text:
The process for remotely distributing avatars is much simpler, as it does not require a custom settings descriptor.

  • In the Project window, locate the avatar prefab you wish to distribute remotely.
  • Drag and drop your avatar prefab into your remote group (e.g., MyRemoteAssets).
  • Crucial Step: In the Address field, you must set the name to match the unique alphanumeric ID that users will use to unlock or load this avatar in the VRUnited avatar selector. It does not need to match the filename.
  • With the avatar selected in the Addressables Groups window, click the dropdown in the Labels column and apply the VRUAvatar label. This critical step ensures the main project identifies the asset as a playable character.

docs.title: 9. Build Addressables
docs.text:
Before pushing your assets to the cloud, you must compile them locally. This process generates the .bundle files, remote catalogs, and hashes required by the Addressables system.

  • Open the Addressables Groups window (Window > Asset Management > Addressables > Groups).
  • If you have built assets previously, it is highly recommended to first click Build > Clean Build > All to clear out old data and prevent conflicts.
  • Click on Build > New Build > Default Build Script to start the compilation.
  • Wait for the process to finish. Unity will automatically generate the files and store them in your local ServerData/[BuildTarget] directory (e.g., ServerData/StandaloneWindows64).
  • Crucial Step: You must repeat this build process for every platform you want to support. Go to File > Build Profiles (or Build Settings), select your next target platform (e.g., Android), click Switch Platform, and then run the Build > New Build > Default Build Script command again.

docs.title: 10. Uploading to CCD
docs.text:
Once your assets are built locally, the final step is to upload them to your Unity Cloud bucket using the web dashboard.

  • Open your web browser and navigate to the Unity Cloud Dashboard.
  • On the left menu, select Cloud Content Delivery and open your specific bucket (e.g., MyRemoteEnvironments).
  • Click the Upload Content option.
  • Open your local file explorer and navigate to your Unity project's ServerData directory.
  • Crucial Step: Select the entire platform folder you just built (e.g., the StandaloneWindows64 folder itself, not the files inside it) and drag and drop it into the Unity Cloud Dashboard drop area. This ensures the logical path is maintained so Android and Windows files do not overwrite each other.

  • Once the upload finishes, you must click the blue Create Release button. This step is mandatory to package your uploaded files into an official version and automatically update the latest badge so VRUnited can detect them.
  • A confirmation dialog will appear. Click Next or Submit to finalize the release.
  • Repeat: You must repeat this build, upload, and release process for every other platform you need (e.g., build for Android, then drag and drop the Android folder into the dashboard).

docs.title: Setting Up Unity Cloud Content Delivery
docs.text: Before configuring any Unity project, the cloud infrastructure must be properly set up in the Unity Dashboard. VRUnited uses Unity Cloud Content Delivery (CCD) to host and distribute Addressables globally without the need for a dedicated web server.

docs.title: Creating the Project and Enabling CCD
docs.text:
Unity Cloud Content Delivery features a generous free tier ideal for development and moderate traffic. Cloud Storage and Content Management are completely free, and you get 50 GB of free bandwidth per month.

To activate the service, Unity requires a valid credit or debit card. This is a standard procedure to verify identity and enable usage-based services. A small temporary hold may be placed on your card, but it will be released automatically. The initial checkout amount is $0.00.

Follow these steps to create your project and activate the service:

  • Log into the Unity Cloud Dashboard.
  • In the Projects section, click on + New.
  • Enter your project name (e.g., MyVRUnitedProject) and click Create.

  • Once inside your new project's dashboard, navigate to the left sidebar and select Cloud Content Delivery.
  • Click the Launch button to start the setup process.
  • On the product details page, click Continue to purchase.
  • Accept the Terms and Conditions, then click Continue to checkout.
  • Enter your billing details and complete the checkout process to fully enable the CCD environment.

With the project created and CCD activated, you are now ready to configure your secondary projects (Producers) to start uploading content to the cloud.

docs.title: FAQ & Account Management
docs.text:
What happens if my application exceeds the 50 GB free tier in a month?

Unity does not currently offer an automatic "hard cap" feature to block downloads once the limit is reached. If your users download more than 50 GB, the service will not be interrupted, and Unity will automatically charge your card for the excess data at the end of the month (currently around $0.08 per additional GB).

Tip: To avoid unexpected charges, it is highly recommended to set up Budget Alerts in the Unity Dashboard (Administration > Billing). You can configure it to send you an email alert as soon as your monthly cost exceeds $0, allowing you to manually disable the content if you do not wish to pay for extra bandwidth.

How can I change the credit card associated with the project (e.g., from a personal to a corporate card)?

You cannot change the card directly from the CCD tab. You must update it at the organization level:

  1. Ensure your organization is selected in the top-right corner.
  2. Go to Manage organization > Administration > Billing & cost > Payment methods.
  3. Click Add payment method and enter the new card details.
  4. Click the three dots (...) next to the new card and select Set as default.
  5. Once the new card is the default, you can delete your old personal card.
How do I completely cancel the CCD service to avoid any future charges?

Since CCD uses usage-based billing, there is no traditional "Cancel Subscription" button. To guarantee a $0 bill, you must reduce your usage and storage to zero:

  1. Delete all Buckets: Go to your project's CCD settings, enter each bucket, and click Delete Bucket. This stops all downloads and clears your storage.
  2. Revoke Access: Go to Administration > Service Accounts and delete the accounts used for CCD (e.g., ccd-manager) to prevent any further API connections.
  3. Remove Payment Method: (Optional) If your organization does not use other paid Unity services, go to Billing & cost > Payment methods and remove the card.

docs.title: Official Documentation
docs.text: For more in-depth information, you can refer to the official Unity guides: * Unity Cloud Content Delivery (CCD) Documentation * Unity Cloud Billing & Organizations

docs.title: VRUnited Template Setup Guide
docs.text: Follow these steps to download, configure, and build your custom VRUnited project.

docs.title: 1. Download VRUnited Template
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the desired directory on your computer where you want to clone the project (create the directory if it does not exist yet).

  2. Clone the repository using the command line or your preferred Git client (e.g., TortoiseGit). You can clone the project using either of the following methods:

    • SSH:

      git@gitlab.com:vrunited/VRUMain.git

    • HTTPS:

      https://gitlab.com/vrunited/VRUMain.git

docs.title: 2. Open Project in Unity
docs.text:
• Open Unity Hub, click Add, and locate your newly cloned project folder to open it. The template currently runs on Unity 6000.0.4f1.

Note: Depending on your specific Unity version, plugin updates, or previous configurations, you may or may not see the following prompts when the editor loads. If they appear, follow the instructions below. If they do not appear, it is not a blocking issue—simply proceed to the next section.

  • If a prompt appears asking to "Enable Meta XR Features", click Yes.

  • If the Project Setup Tool window opens showing recommended fixes, click Fix All in the bottom right corner to automatically resolve missing configuration settings.

docs.title: 3. Configure Photon (PUN & Voice)
docs.text:
• In Unity, navigate to the top menu and select Window > Photon Unity Networking > PUN Wizard, then click Highlight Server Settings.
  • This will highlight the PhotonServerSettings asset in your project, which is used internally by Photon to configure the application.
  • Select this file to view its properties in the Inspector. In the Server/Cloud Settings section, you will find the App Id PUN and App Id Voice fields. These IDs basically identify the multiplayer and voice projects within the Photon servers to synchronize the virtual world and voice transmission.
  • Click the Dashboard button next to any of the App Id fields. This will automatically open your web browser and take you to your Photon dashboard.
  • Create the PUN App: Click Create a New App, set the Photon SDK to Pun, enter an Application Name (e.g., MyVRUnitedProject), and click Create.
  • Create the Voice App: Click Create a New App again, set the Photon SDK to Voice, enter an Application Name (e.g., MyVRUnitedProject_Voice), and click Create.
  • From your dashboard, copy the App ID of your new PUN application and paste it into the App Id PUN field within Unity's PhotonServerSettings inspector.
  • Repeat the process to get the App ID of the Voice application, and enter this ID into the App Id Voice field in the PhotonServerSettings inspector.

docs.title: 4. Check VR Configuration
docs.text:
• Go to Edit > Project Settings and select XR Plug-in Management from the left sidebar.
  • Under the Android tab, ensure that the OpenXR plug-in provider is checked. Ensure that the OpenXR plug-in provider is also checked under the Desktop tab.
  • Click on OpenXR under the XR Plug-in Management dropdown. Under the Desktop tab, add any interaction profiles you need to support for your specific case (Meta Quest, HTC Vive, Valve Index, etc.).
  • In the OpenXR Feature Groups section, ensure that the following options are enabled (checked): Get System Info, Hand Tracking Subsystem, and Meta Hand Tracking Aim.
  • Similarly, configure the Android platform. Ensure that in the Interaction Profiles section, you have added all the controller types that your application will support.
  • In the OpenXR Feature Groups section for the Android platform, ensure that you select Hand Tracking Subsystem and Meta Hand Tracking Aim.

docs.title: 5. Switch Profile and Update Player Settings
docs.text:
• Navigate to File > Build Profiles.
  • Select the Meta Quest profile from the list and click Switch Platform. Wait for Unity to recompile the scripts and compress assets.
  • Go to Edit > Project Settings and select Player.
  • Update the Company Name and Product Name to match your specific project details.
  • Scroll down to Publishing Settings and check the Keystore Manager. Select your custom keystore file and enter the required Keystore password and Key password.
  • In the Project window, use the search bar to find the AndroidManifest file. It is located in Assets > Plugins > Android.
  • Open the file with your default code editor and, on the second line, change the package name to match the company and product name you defined previously.

docs.title: 6. Build the Project
docs.text:
• Return to File > Build Profiles. Click Build.
  • Select the location where you want to generate the build. (Note: Creating a specific Builds folder inside your project directory is highly recommended to keep things organized, but you can save it anywhere you prefer).
  • Name your file (e.g., MyVRUnitedProject.apk) and click Save.
  • If a warning prompt appears stating "Missing Project ID", click Yes to continue.
  • Wait for the build process to complete. Your APK is now ready to be deployed to your headset.
